## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Saṅgīti Sutta* ("Reciting in Concert", DN 33) is the thirty-third discourse of the *Dīghanikāya* [SuttaCentral]. Set in the context of the factional disputes that broke out among the Jains following the death of their leader Nāthaputta at Pāvā, the sutta was delivered by Venerable Sāriputta with the Buddha's encouragement as a precautionary measure to preserve doctrinal unity and prevent schism within the Buddhist Sangha [SuttaCentral; Norman 1983]. The discourse functions as an extensive mnemonic compilation of doctrinal categories arranged in ascending numerical groups from ones to tens [Norman 1983; Williams 2005]. Because of its technical style, overlapping categories (such as treating both the five aggregates and five grasping aggregates), and resemblance to the Abhidhamma *mātikā*s, scholars regard it as a late canonical addition marking the transition from the early sūtra period to the beginnings of Abhidharma literature [Norman 1983; Gaffney 2003; Analayo 2014].
The sutta is extensively represented across Buddhist canonical traditions. Extant parallels include Sanskrit manuscript fragments of the *Saṅgītisūtra* recovered from Central Asia and Bamiyan, as well as Chinese translations in the *Dīrghāgama* (DĀ 9) and separate versions such as T 12 and T 13 [SuttaCentral; Norman 1983; Nakamura 1980; Potter 1996]. It also served as the root text for the Sarvāstivāda Abhidharma work *Saṅgītiparyāya* (extant in Chinese and Sanskrit fragments) [Potter 1996; Norman 1983]. Curated parallels and DharmaNexus text-reuse matches demonstrate substantial shared material across the canon, sharing thousands of characters most extensively with its direct sequel the *Dasuttara Sutta* (DN 34), several divisions of the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* (AN 3–AN 11), the *Khuddakavatthuvibhaṅga* (Vb 17), and the *Mahāparinibbāna Sutta* (DN 16), along with cross-language alignments with Sanskrit fragments (SF 253) and Chinese *Dīrghāgama* texts [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus].
